title: Evidence, notes and handoffs
summary: Rewrite a poor helpdesk ticket into a triage note, an escalation and a shift handover that the next analyst can act on, using the evidence from a real phishing case.
rubric: Triage note: alert ID, time with time zone, and what was checked, so someone else can repeat it
Triage note: facts with times and sources, kept apart from guesses
Triage note: a disposition with one sentence of reasons
Escalation: the ask in the first line, with who and by when
Escalation: what we know, what we don't know, and impact
Escalation: where the evidence is saved
Shift handover: every open item by ID, with the next step and owner
Shift handover: things to watch and calls made, with times
Plain writing: short sentences, no blame, no guessing presented as fact
handin: A triage note for AL-3303, an escalation, and a shift handover for the Saffron case (download each from the report builder, or hand in this notebook).

script.intro: Hello, and welcome to Evidence, notes and handoffs, the free foundation seminar. I'm going to start with a confession about this job. Most of the work in a security team isn't hacking and it isn't clever tools. It's writing things down so the next person can act. A ticket goes from the helpdesk to the SOC. An alert goes from the SOC to the incident lead. The night shift hands over to the morning shift. Every one of those handoffs is a moment where an attack can slip through, because the note was vague, or had no times, or mixed up facts with guesses. So today we take one real case, a fake invoice that turned into ransomware at a freight company called Kestrel Logistics, and one helpdesk ticket that nobody can use. Over the next twenty minutes you'll rewrite it three ways: as a triage note, as an escalation, and as a shift handover. By the end, you'll have three pieces of writing that any analyst could pick up and act on. Everything runs in your browser, in the notebook on your screen. Let's start where the analyst starts: with the ticket.

steps.say: Step one: a ticket nobody can act on. It's Monday the second of November 2026, at Kestrel Logistics. All the times in this case are in UTC, and India is five and a half hours ahead, so 09:00 UTC is 2:30 in the afternoon in India. Keep that in mind, because mixing time zones is the most common mistake in incident notes. The Linux cell prints two notes: helpdesk ticket 88213, and last night's shift handover. Read them the way the next person would, someone who wasn't there and has to decide what to do in the next five minutes.
steps.after: Let's look closely. The ticket was opened automatically at 09:16, when dev.kapoor pressed the Report phishing button on message 4A1F21C02. That's a real fact, with a time and a source. Then Ramesh from the helpdesk writes: user says got weird invoice email, probably spam, told her to delete it. Notice three problems in that one line. Which user? Probably spam is a guess. And told her to delete it means he asked someone to destroy the evidence. Next line: HR PC slow, three question marks, maybe virus, will check later. Another guess, and later is not a time. Then: someone said files on share have funny names, not sure if related. That's the most important line in the whole ticket, files being renamed is what ransomware does, and it's written as an afterthought. Finally, at 09:52, he pulled the cable on the HR PC. That was the right thing to do, but there's no time zone and no host name. Now the night handover: all quiet, couple of alerts, nothing major, printer thing again, AV update failed somewhere, think it fixed itself, someone on VPN from Singapore, didn't check. Not one alert ID, not one host, and a lead that was left for nobody. Here's the test I want you to remember for every note you ever write. A useful note answers five questions: what fired, what I checked, what I found, what I don't know yet, and what happens next. This ticket answers almost none of them. Answer the two questions: the message ID is 4A1F21C02, and the cable was pulled at 09:52.

steps.say: Step two: find the facts behind the ticket. A good note is built from evidence, not from what someone said on the phone. We'll check two logs. First mail.log, the mail server's delivery log. In it, nrcpt means the number of recipients, and each to line is one mailbox. Then proxy.log, the web proxy, which records every download. In the proxy log, TCP_MISS slash 200 means the download worked, and TCP_DENIED slash 403 means the proxy blocked it. One more thing: proxy times are Unix epoch seconds, a count of seconds since 1970. The Python cell turns them into ordinary UTC clock times, so every fact in your note uses the same clock.
steps.after: The mail log tells us message 4A1F21C02 arrived at 08:51 from bounce at kestrel-logistlcs.com. Read that domain slowly: logistlcs, with an L where the i should be. It went to three people: priya.nair, dev.kapoor and tomas.reyes. At 09:15 dev.kapoor reported it, and at 09:18 the proxy's blocklist was updated with the fake domain. Now the proxy. At 09:02:31 UTC, 10.20.0.14 downloaded INV-30412.docm, a Word document with macros. At 09:03:09 the same address downloaded s2.bin from cdn-update-check.net, a program. And at 09:20:47, 10.20.0.15, the Finance laptop, tried to download the same invoice and was denied, because the blocklist had gone in two minutes earlier. Look how much we now know that the ticket didn't say. Three recipients, one download, one blocked attempt, and a second download that wasn't an invoice at all. And every fact has a time and a file name, so anyone can check it. Answer the questions: three people received it, and 10.20.0.14 downloaded it.

steps.say: Step three: what ran on the PC. The ticket said HR PC slow, maybe virus. That's a guess. The process list from the company's endpoint tool says exactly what ran, when, and which program started it. Every process has a PID, its own number, and a ppid, the number of its parent. The Python cell builds the family tree for hr-pc07, so you can follow it from top to bottom.
steps.after: Here's the chain. At 09:02:41, WINWORD.EXE opens INV-30412.docm from Priya's Downloads folder. At 09:02:55, Word starts cmd.exe, with a command that starts PowerShell minimised. Ask yourself: should a word processor ever start a command prompt? No. That's the macro running. One second later, PowerShell starts with the window hidden and runs a script from C:\Users\Public. At 09:03:20 PowerShell starts svchost-upd.exe, PID 4810, from the same Public folder. The real svchost.exe lives in C:\Windows\System32 and runs as SYSTEM. A file called svchost-upd.exe in a folder everyone can write to is pretending to be a Windows program. And at 09:41 that same program starts again with the arguments walk Z drive, extension kestrel-locked, note README_RESTORE.txt. Z is the mapped file share. That's the moment the encryption began. So the facts are: Word, then cmd, then hidden PowerShell, then the malware, and forty minutes later, the share. Answer the questions: WINWORD.EXE started cmd.exe, and the malware's PID is 4810.

steps.say: Step four: write the triage note. Now we rewrite ticket 88213 as a proper triage note for alert AL-2203, the macro document alert. The report builder on your screen checks each section as you type. It wants an alert ID, times with a time zone, the exact searches you ran, at least one gap, a disposition and an owner. Three rules make notes useful. One time zone for everything, UTC here, written every single time. Facts say where you saw them, and guesses go in their own section called what I don't know yet. And write what you ran, so the next person can repeat it without having to ask you.
steps.after: Here's the model note. What fired: AL-2203, Office document with macros opened from the internet, severity high, host hr-pc07, user priya.nair, at 09:02:44 UTC. What I checked: the exact grep on mail.log for the message ID, the grep on proxy.log for the document and the download, and the process tree for hr-pc07. What I found: each fact from steps two and three, with its time and its file. What I don't know yet: did the other two recipients open the invoice, and was anything copied out? That section is never empty, and writing it down is what stops the next person assuming everything has been checked. Then the disposition, escalate, and the owner. When you try it yourself, write your own note first and only then compare it with the model. And download the Markdown: it's part of your hand-in. Answer the question: the disposition for AL-2203 is escalate.

steps.say: Step five: escalate. An escalation is read in about ten seconds, often by someone who has just been woken up. So the first line is the ask: what you need, from whom, and by when. After that comes the severity and the one fact that decided it, then what you know, what you don't know, the impact, what you did, and where the evidence is. And one thing beginners forget: say what you have not done. I have not changed anything on the host tells the incident lead the evidence is still clean. The Linux cell counts the encrypted files on the share and hashes the evidence, so you can say exactly what you saved.
steps.after: The share listing was taken at 09:58, after the cable was pulled. The HR folder has six files renamed to .kestrel-locked, between 09:41 and 09:42, and a ransom note. The Finance folder has four more, between 09:47 and 09:50: the ledger, vendor bank details, GST returns and the budget. That's ten encrypted files, and the Ops folder is untouched, because the cable was pulled before the malware reached it. The hashes give us a fingerprint of every evidence file, so later we can prove nothing changed. Now read the model escalation. The ask: please open a critical incident and approve isolating hr-pc07 and taking the HR and Finance shares read-only, by 10:05 UTC. Severity: critical, because files are being encrypted right now. That's the deciding fact. Then the timeline from 08:51 to 09:52, each line with its source. What we don't know: the other two recipients, whether data was copied out, and whether the attacker can reach any other host. The impact: payroll and vendor bank details, which are personal data. And the evidence, saved with hashes. Answer the questions: ten files were encrypted, and the Ops folder was not.

steps.say: Step six: work the queue before you hand over. Your shift had ten alerts, and the night shift left a note that said nothing major. Before you hand over, every alert needs a disposition and one line of reason that a stranger could check. Some alerts belong to the incident. Some are ordinary noise and should be closed, so the next shift doesn't waste an hour chasing them. The alert queue on your screen sorts by severity, then by time. Pick an alert, choose a disposition, and write why.
steps.after: Here's how the queue works out. Seven alerts belong to this incident and get escalated: AL-2201, the email from the look-alike domain; AL-2203, the macro document; AL-2204, a scheduled task that runs the malware every time someone logs on; AL-2205, the download of s2.bin; AL-2210, a new local administrator called support_svc; AL-2208, the mass rename on the file share; and AL-2207, failed logons from outside for support_svc and Administrator. Three are benign. AL-2202 looks scary, an impossible-travel sign-in from Singapore, but read the detail line: the Singapore address is the company's own VPN exit. AL-2206, the antivirus update, failed and then worked on retry at 09:25. And AL-2209 is a 412-page print job, which is a lot of paper but not an attack. Closing those three with a clear reason is just as valuable as escalating the other seven. Answer the questions: AL-2202 is the VPN exit, and the account the attacker created is support_svc.

steps.say: Step seven: write the shift handover. Now rewrite last night's all quiet note as a handover that leaves nothing behind. Every open item by ID, with the next step and who owns it. What you closed, one line each. What the next shift should watch for. Who you called and when. And any temporary change, like a block, that someone must review or undo later.
steps.after: Here's the model handover. Still open: INC-0211, the incident made from five of the alerts, contained at 09:52, with the next step, a restore decision, and the owner, IT operations. AL-2201, same campaign: confirm whether dev.kapoor and tomas.reyes opened the invoice, owned by the afternoon analyst, by 14:00 UTC. AL-2207, the failed logons: confirm support_svc is disabled, owned by IT ops. Closed this shift: the three benign alerts, each with its reason. Watch for: any connection to 198.51.100.140 or cdn-update-check.net, any new account called support_svc, and any new file ending in kestrel-locked. Calls: the escalation by phone at 09:55, and a message to IT ops at 10:02, answered at 10:06. And the temporary proxy blocks, with a review date of the ninth of November and who may remove them. A temporary block nobody remembers becomes a permanent one. Compare that with all quiet, couple of alerts. The afternoon shift can start work the moment they read it.

steps.say: Step eight: hand in. You hand in three pieces of writing: the triage note for AL-2203, the escalation, and the shift handover. Your teacher marks them with the rubric on your screen, and your certificate is issued once the hand-in is scored. Use the Hand in button at the top of the notebook, and your notes, your tool work and your answers go with it.
steps.after: Before you press it, one last habit. Read each piece aloud, once. If any sentence needs you to explain it, rewrite it, because you won't be there when someone else reads it. Look at the rubric: most of the points are for the boring parts, the time zones, the sources, the owners, the IDs. That's on purpose. Those are the parts that make a note useful at three in the morning.

script.outro: That's the seminar. You started with a ticket that said probably spam and maybe virus, and you turned it into three documents an analyst can act on: a triage note with facts, times and sources; an escalation that puts the ask first; and a handover that leaves nothing behind. Remember the five questions: what fired, what I checked, what I found, what I don't know yet, and what happens next. Use one time zone, write down what you ran, and keep facts and guesses apart. These habits matter in every security job, from the SOC to the boardroom. When you're ready, the next seminar, Reading evidence, takes you into packets, Linux and Windows logs. Thank you for watching, and well done.

# Evidence, notes and handoffs (Practice)

Practice: a new case with the same skills. Saffron Pharma Distributors, a medicine wholesaler in Ahmedabad, on Tuesday 10 November 2026. A fake courier email, a script in a zip file, and files locked on the share. Fewer hints than the walkthrough: use what you learned there. All times are UTC unless a question says IST.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `alerts.json`, `courier.eml`, `handover-night.txt`, `mail.log`, `process.csv`, `proxy.log`, `README.txt`, `share_listing.txt`, `ticket-55120.txt`.

## 1. A ticket nobody can act on

A new case: Saffron Pharma Distributors, a medicine wholesaler in Ahmedabad, on Tuesday 10 November 2026. The habits are the ones from the walkthrough. The evidence is new, and there are fewer hints.

Read helpdesk ticket 55120 and last night's handover the way the next person would: someone who wasn't there and has five minutes to decide.

- [ ] Which facts in the ticket have a time and a source?
- [ ] Which words are guesses?
- [ ] Which line matters most, and why is it written as an afterthought?
- [ ] What would the next shift need from last night's handover that it doesn't say?

?> Which message ID did arjun.rao report as phishing? :: sha256:8c6aeebc43859e7dfc90ae187108e983c9c9ea5a6014fa80be77c636d69f8fe2
?> How many minutes after the ticket was opened did the helpdesk unplug the laptop? (a number) :: sha256:44cb730c420480a0477b505ae68af508fb90f96cf0ec54c6ad16949dd427f13a
?> The laptop was unplugged at 11:14 UTC. What time was that in India? (HH:MM, IST) :: sha256:f1aa7e2c74c034b3fe734f294220c524a88a987941102517f45684bc821c8110

## 2. Find the facts behind the ticket

Build the note from the logs, not from what someone said on the phone. Start with the reported message in mail.log, then find every download in proxy.log that came from it, and what came after.

- [ ] Who received the email, and when?
- [ ] Which internal address downloaded the archive, and was anyone blocked?
- [ ] What did the same address download next, and what does it keep doing?
- [ ] Write each fact with its UTC time and the file you saw it in

?> Which internal IP address downloaded the archive successfully? :: sha256:322a64ce11cf896ec075c6b580a5c5b6e6122051d05a4b13508767fc23000237
?> How many encrypted (CONNECT, TCP_TUNNEL) sessions did that address open to files-cdn-sync.example? :: sha256:e7f6c011776e8db7cd330b54174fd76f7d0216b612387a5ffcfb81e6f0919683
?> How many seconds apart are those sessions? :: sha256:284b7e6d788f363f910f7beb1910473e23ce9d6c871f1ce0f31f22a982d48ad4

template.a:
cd ~/case
grep 7C3E90B14 mail.log
echo ---
grep -E 'report|blocklist' mail.log
echo ---
grep -E 'AWB-77120|upd.dat|files-cdn-sync' proxy.log

## 3. What ran on the PC

"Nothing happened, closed a popup" is what the user saw. The process list says what really ran on acct-lt04. Follow the `ppid` column from explorer.exe down.

- [ ] Which program ran the file from the archive? Should a "PDF" ever be run by it?
- [ ] Where does the program PowerShell started live? Where does the real OneDrive live on the same laptop?
- [ ] What did that program do in its first minute?
- [ ] When did it reach the file share?

?> Which program started cmd.exe? (file name) :: sha256:d7d5da6e68ec38fef2769347ca16ca02e70cffcff3efdfdace89631a309f839f
?> What is the PID of the OneDriveSync.exe that PowerShell started? :: sha256:43219ea99d4f6b23a85b1c0276ba48a3e6b8ce1e8a2131632f18643882f948ce
?> How many seconds after the script ran did OneDriveSync.exe start? :: sha256:031b4af5197ec30a926f48cf40e11a7dbc470048a21e4003b7a3c07c5dab1baa
?> Which account did the attacker add to Administrators? :: sha256:20531e8211d31302a070348684fafdc579050391209f64d0c51e0504217d7406

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with import.
template.a:
import csv
from collections import defaultdict

rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(open("case/process.csv")) if r["host"] == "acct-lt04"]
kids = defaultdict(list)
for r in rows:
    kids[r["ppid"]].append(r)


def show(pid, depth):
    for r in kids.get(pid, []):
        print("    " * depth + r["time"][11:] + " UTC  " + r["image"].split("\\")[-1] + "  (pid " + r["pid"] + ")  " + r["command_line"][:60])
        show(r["pid"], depth + 1)


show("690", 0)

## 4. Write the triage note

Write a triage note for alert **AL-3303**, the script run from the downloaded archive. The report builder checks each section: alert ID, times with a time zone, the exact searches you ran, at least one gap, a disposition and an owner.

- [ ] Fill every section, then press Check the report
- [ ] Compare yours with the model answer only after you've written your own
- [ ] Download the Markdown: it is part of your hand-in

```tool report
{"tpl": "triage", "title": "Triage note: AL-3303 script from a downloaded archive on acct-lt04", "text": "", "n": 6, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Triage note: AL-3303 script from a downloaded archive on acct-lt04

## What fired

AL-3303 "Script run from a downloaded archive", severity high, host acct-lt04, user meera.shah, 2026-11-10 10:15:41 UTC.

## What I checked

- mail.log: grep 7C3E90B14 (the reported message), and grep -E 'report|blocklist'
- proxy.log: grep -E 'AWB-77120|upd.dat|files-cdn-sync', times turned into UTC (Python cell, step 2)
- process.csv: the process tree for acct-lt04 (Python cell, step 3)
- alerts.json: the other alerts on acct-lt04 between 10:00 and 11:20 UTC

## What I found

- 10:12 UTC: message 7C3E90B14 from noreply@swiftroute-delivery.example (look-alike courier domain, 203.0.113.62) was delivered to 3 people: meera.shah, arjun.rao, kiran.joshi.
- 10:14:58 UTC: 10.30.0.21 downloaded AWB-77120.zip from swiftroute-delivery.example (proxy TCP_MISS/200).
- 10:15:40 UTC: wscript.exe ran AWB-77120.pdf.js from Downloads; it started cmd.exe and a hidden PowerShell running C:\ProgramData\cache\p.ps1.
- 10:16:12 UTC: acct-lt04 downloaded upd.dat from files-cdn-sync.example (198.51.100.77).
- 10:16:31 UTC: PowerShell started C:\ProgramData\cache\OneDriveSync.exe (PID 5302). The real OneDrive.exe runs from C:\Program Files.
- 10:17 UTC: PID 5302 created local account svc_sync and added it to Administrators; PowerShell turned off antivirus real-time protection.
- From 10:16:40 UTC: an encrypted session to files-cdn-sync.example every 600 seconds; the one at 11:06:40 was far larger (88,004 bytes).
- 11:02 UTC: PID 5302 mapped \\fs02\dept and started renaming files to .saffron-locked (AL-3309).

## What I don't know yet

- Whether kiran.joshi opened the archive (arjun.rao's attempt was blocked at 10:36 UTC; there is no proxy line for kiran.joshi).
- What was sent in the larger session at 11:06:40 UTC.
- Whether svc_sync was used anywhere else.

## Disposition and why

True positive, escalate: a script from a look-alike courier's archive started a hidden PowerShell and an unknown program that is now encrypting the file share.

## Next step and owner

Escalate to the incident lead now (11:16 UTC). Owner: SOC analyst on shift until the incident lead takes it; keep acct-lt04 off the network and do not reboot it.
"}}
```

?> Which disposition fits AL-3303? (escalate, handled, benign, false positive or more information) :: sha256:f965e5fbf98dd531b7c0fd4f9bdc8dd6df79f623c8345b8aa1b7cd756d317dd8
?> Which internal IP address is sales-lt11, arjun.rao's laptop? :: sha256:8a58ded49f31b62fb6b9a08a167397458b5cc39316dfb6efc1c42bdb7f736ab7
?> Of the three people who received the email, how many are known to have tried to open the archive? :: sha256:d4735e3a265e16eee03f59718b9b5d03019c07d8b6c51f90da3a666eec13ab35

## 5. Escalate

Write the escalation for the incident lead. The ask goes in the first line, with who and by when. Then severity and the one fact that decided it, what you know, what you don't, impact, what you did (and didn't), and where the evidence is.

- [ ] First line: the ask, with a time
- [ ] Severity, and the one fact that decided it
- [ ] Facts with times, newest last
- [ ] Where the evidence is saved (file names or hashes)

```tool report
{"tpl": "escalation", "title": "Escalation: ransomware on acct-lt04 and fs02", "text": "", "n": 7, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Escalation: ransomware on acct-lt04 and fs02

## The ask

Please open a critical incident and approve keeping acct-lt04 isolated, taking the Accounts and Purchase shares on fs02 read-only and disabling the account svc_sync on vpn01, by 11:30 UTC. Incident lead and IT operations, please call the SOC.

## Severity and why

Critical: files on fs02 were being encrypted (AL-3309), and someone outside is trying the attacker's new account on the VPN (AL-3310).

## What we know

- 10:12 UTC: a fake courier email from swiftroute-delivery.example reached 3 people (mail.log, message 7C3E90B14).
- 10:14:58 UTC: meera.shah on acct-lt04 downloaded AWB-77120.zip; at 10:15:40 wscript.exe ran the .js inside it, which started a hidden PowerShell (proxy.log, process.csv).
- 10:16 UTC: PowerShell downloaded upd.dat from files-cdn-sync.example and started OneDriveSync.exe from C:\ProgramData\cache (proxy.log, process.csv).
- 10:17 UTC: local administrator svc_sync was created and antivirus real-time protection was turned off (AL-3311, AL-3307).
- 11:02 to 11:12 UTC: files on \\fs02\dept\Accounts and \Purchase were renamed to .saffron-locked (share_listing.txt).
- 11:14 UTC: the helpdesk unplugged acct-lt04 (ticket 55120).
- 11:19 UTC: 5 failed VPN logons for svc_sync and Administrator from 198.51.100.77, the same address as the download server (AL-3310).

## What we don't know

- Whether kiran.joshi opened the archive.
- What was sent in the larger session to files-cdn-sync.example at 11:06:40 UTC.
- Whether the attacker has access to any other host.

## Impact so far

Host acct-lt04 and user account meera.shah are compromised. 8 files on the Accounts and Purchase shares are encrypted, including bank reconciliation, salary advances and the supplier master with bank details (personal and financial data). Warehouse is not encrypted. The encryption stopped after the laptop was unplugged.

## What I've done

- 11:14 UTC: the helpdesk unplugged acct-lt04 (not me; I have not changed anything on the host).
- 11:16 UTC: I asked the proxy team to confirm swiftroute-delivery.example and files-cdn-sync.example are blocked.

## Evidence

Saved in the incident folder with SHA-256 hashes: alerts.json, mail.log, proxy.log, process.csv, share_listing.txt and courier.eml. Ticket 55120 holds the helpdesk notes.
"}}
```
